extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematical researchers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for deciding when to continue, revise, scale back, or abandon mathematical research projects and drafts; includes guidance on backups and how to treat failed work. Targeted at people producing mathematical papers and expository writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that not every idea or first draft will succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not every idea leads to a success, and not every first draft forms a good template for the final draft."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is true even for the very best mathematicians; expect many starts to be abandoned or substantially reworked rather than taken through to final publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale down, refocus, or shelve projects that are not working
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are times when a project just isn’t working the way it was initially planned, and you have to scale it down, refocus it, or shelve it altogether; or a lemma that you spent a lot of time on turns out not to add anything much to the paper and has to be reluctantly jettisoned or deferred to another paper; or that the structure of a half-written paper is clearly not optimal and that one needs to rewrite the entire thing from scratch."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete actions include removing or deferring lemmas, rewriting the paper from scratch, narrowing the scope, or shelving the project until tools/understanding improve; recognise structural problems early rather than tacking on fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to perform complete rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: "Indeed, some of the papers I am most proud of are virtually unrecognizable from their first draft, due to one or more complete rewrites."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A major rewrite can be necessary for quality; do not treat the first draft as sacred. Consider rewriting when structure or exposition is poor rather than incrementally patching a flawed draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance persistence with pragmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: "One has to know when one should be persistent and patient, and when one should be pragmatic and realistic; stubbornly working away at a dead end is not the most efficient use of your time, and publishing every last scrap of your work is not always the best way to meet the standards of quality you expect from your publications (though sometimes it is still worth making your partial successes available in some format)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh continuing a difficult line of attack versus reallocating time to more promising problems; avoid inefficiently pursuing dead ends, but consider sharing partial results (e.g., notes, preprints) when they can be useful to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backup work before major edits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of course, in today’s digital age it is cheap and easy to backup all your work, and you should certainly do this before performing major surgery on any paper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regular digital backups (versioned where possible) so that discarded material can be recovered if needed; use this safety net when undertaking large structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archive wrong or embarrassing work privately for future salvage and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: "Even an embarrassingly wrong piece of work (and I have a number of these, which fortunately have never made it as far as publication) should be stored privately somewhere, because you never know whether something salvageable can be extracted from it, and also it is good to make a note of mistakes that one should avoid in the future."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep private archives of failed drafts and mistakes to extract salvageable ideas later and to learn the limitations of your methods and tools; avoid publishing clear errors but retain them for personal learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use failures to learn the limitations of your tools
rubrics_metrics.description: "For instance, it can help you learn the limitations of your own tools."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat failed approaches as diagnostics: record why they failed, which assumptions or tools were insufficient, and use that knowledge to guide future problem selection or method development.
